Modern Web Guidance (Source)
This repo is the source repository for GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance and includes the code and documentation for authoring, calibrating, and evaluating its contents.
*Modern Web Guidance** is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.
See CONTRIBUTING.md and GOVERNANCE.md for how we work on the project and orientation of the codebase.
--
Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.*
Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue
Quickstart
npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below.
Try it out (without installing)
Search for relevant guides
npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop"
Retrieve a guide by ID
npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer"
Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize
npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan .
Why?
Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions.
Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code.
*Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap.** Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on:
**Modern Browser APIs**: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse.
**Performance & Accessibility**: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances.
**Responsible Fallbacks**: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries.
What's Included?
We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are **designed to be token-efficient**; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know.
Core Disciplines
🎨 User Experience
Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color).
📐 CSS Layout
Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid, modern color spaces like oklch, text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).
⚡ Performance
Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield).
📝 Forms & UI
Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).
♿ Accessibility
Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).
🤖 Built-in AI
Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).
_View an example:_ the navigation-drawer guide.

Codex Security
Codex Security helps you find, investigate, and fix vulnerabilities in your code.
Use its security workflows in Codex, or automate them with the
@openai/codex-security CLI and TypeScript SDK.
**In Codex:** choose a security workflow.
**In a terminal:** install the CLI and scan your repository.
**In automation:** use the TypeScript SDK or
GitHub Action.
Features
Scan repositories, selected paths, or Git changes. Deep scans repeat Standard scans and return their deduplicated findings.
Validate candidate findings, generate patches, and verify existing fixes.
Draft SECURITY.md policies and save threat models for later review.
Browse saved scans and findings, identify duplicates, assess severity against
your own rubric, and suggest owners from source and Git history.
Preview third-party scanner findings, save them locally, or publish supported reports to Codex Security Cloud. Scanner import guides.
Track findings in Linear, Jira, or GitHub, publish completed scans, or export SARIF, JSON, and CSV. Integration workflows.
Automate scans across repositories or project components, including in CI and
containers.
Use in Codex
Open your repository in a Codex session with the Codex Security plugin enabled,
then ask:
> Run a Codex Security scan on this repository, focusing on authentication and
> authorization. Return the saved report, source evidence, and coverage limits.
A completed scan saves a report and findings. Read the report for source
evidence and exclusions, then request a patch or ask Codex to verify an
existing fix. See the agent workflow guide for setup,
task selection, and recovery.
Quick start
Requires Node.js 22.13.0+ within 22.x, or Node.js 24.x or 26.x, and Python 3.10+.
Python 3.10 also requires tomli.
Install the CLI globally and sign in:
npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login
Run your first scan from the repository directory:
cs scan .
When the scan completes, open the Markdown file at the **REPORT** path in the
terminal. Run cs scans show from the same repository to find its latest
completed scan again. See scan scope and follow-up work
for how to interpret exclusions in the report.
cs and codex-security run the same CLI. If the short name conflicts with
another command, use codex-security. To skip the global install, or if npm
reports an EEXIST conflict, use npx @openai/codex-security in place of
cs for both login and scanning.
For CI, set OPENAI_API_KEY or CODEX_API_KEY in the scan process's environment.
For a headless machine, see device or SSH login.
Scan options
Choose a scope and scan mode:
Scan selected paths.
cs scan . --path src --path tests
Scan committed changes from a base revision to HEAD.
cs scan . --diff origin/main
Run a deep scan of the repository.
cs scan . --mode deep
Use cs scan . --max-time 15 for an advisory 15-minute Standard investigation
allowance. See investigation time
for timing semantics and Deep Scan limits.
Use cs --help to browse commands, or cs scan --help
for scan options, cost limits, and patching after a scan.
For an application spread across repositories, see
review one system across repositories.
Use bulk scans for independent repository
reviews in one resumable campaign.
Scans use existing root and component SECURITY.md guidance. To write or
revise it, see Generate SECURITY.md.
Some cybersecurity requests and protected findings require
Trusted Access for Cyber. For accounts with Daybreak
access, see Daybreak opt-in for the
Codex toggle and Cyber access programs
to select a program explicitly.

HermesEnabler 2
English · Tiếng Việt · 한국어 · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語 · Español · Français · Deutsch · Português
> Supported only on watchOS 27.0 through 27.3 beta 1.
Installation
macOS
On macOS you can install the prebuilt IPA with Sideloadly or build the app directly with Xcode. Either way, the iPhone must be paired with the target Apple Watch, and the Watch must run a supported watchOS version.
Install the IPA
> **Known issue with Sideloadly 0.72:** Issue #43 reports that this version may remove the embedded Watch app while signing. If the iPhone app installs but HermesEnabler2 is missing from the Watch, use Xcode instead. This report is specific to version 0.72; compatibility with other versions has not been confirmed.
1. Download the IPA from Releases.
2. Install Sideloadly on your Mac, connect your iPhone with a cable, and select it in Sideloadly.
3. Drag the IPA into Sideloadly and enter your Apple ID. Turn off **Use automatic bundle ID**, set a fixed Bundle Identifier, and start signing.
4. On the iPhone, open **Settings → General → VPN & Device Management** and trust your developer certificate.
5. On the iPhone, open **Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Mode**, turn it on, restart, and confirm.
6. On the iPhone, open the **Watch** app, go to **My Watch → Apps**, and install **HermesEnabler2** on the Watch.
7. On the Apple Watch, open **Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Mode**, turn it on, restart, and confirm. If the option is not shown, install the Watch app first and check again.
8. Open **HermesEnabler2** on your Apple Watch and follow the steps in the app.
Build with Xcode
1. Open HermesEnabler2.xcodeproj in Xcode.
2. Select your Apple Watch as the run destination and click **Run**.
3. Open **HermesEnabler2** on your Apple Watch and follow the steps in the app.
Windows
Windows uses WatchBridge, a community tool that prepares Developer Mode and installs an IPA containing both an iPhone host app and a Watch app. It is not affiliated with Apple or with this project.
1. Install **Apple Mobile Device Service** by installing iTunes or the **Apple Devices** app from the Microsoft Store. WatchBridge needs it for USB and Wi-Fi communication. WebView2 is built into Windows 11.
2. Make sure your iPhone is paired with the target Apple Watch. WatchBridge supports only one paired Watch at a time; if more than one is paired, the preparation step stops instead of guessing.
3. Download watchbridge-windows.zip from WatchBridge Releases, extract it, and run WatchBridge.exe. The executable is unsigned, so Windows SmartScreen may warn on first launch.
4. Download the IPA from Releases. Use the original IPA that contains both the iPhone host and the Watch/*.app; Watch-only packages are not supported.
5. Connect the paired iPhone over USB and select it in WatchBridge.
6. Pair the Watch and confirm the trust prompt on the Watch. Request the **Developer Mode** switch, then on the Watch open **Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Mode**, turn it on, restart, and confirm. Return to WatchBridge and click **Check again**. WatchBridge does not enable Developer Mode or restart the Watch for you.
7. Sign in with your Apple ID, select the HermesEnabler2 IPA, and start signing and installation. WatchBridge installs the iPhone host app first, then the Watch app.
8. Open **HermesEnabler2** on your Apple Watch and follow the steps in the app.
> Developer-mode preparation requires a USB connection. After pairing over USB once, installs and renewals can use Wi-Fi.
Cautions
In Sideloadly, disable **Use automatic bundle ID** and use a fixed Bundle Identifier. Keep the same Bundle Identifier and Apple ID for every update so the app can retain its existing data and backup.
Free Apple Personal Team provisioning profiles expire after seven days. When that happens, rebuild and reinstall the app, using the same Apple ID and Bundle Identifier.
This project uses an **App Groups** entitlement, which a free Personal Team cannot provision. A paid developer team may be required; changing the Bundle Identifier does not remove this limitation. Do not assume that removing the entitlement is a complete fix, as the app's main functionality without it has not been confirmed.
If the iPhone app installs but the Watch app does not appear, check the Sideloadly log for Watch apps will be stripped from the IPA. This means the embedded Watch app was removed; installing the iPhone app alone will not install it. Use Xcode to install the Watch app.
Before deleting the app, always restore your MobileGestalt backup through the HermesEnabler2 app.
Credits
This project incorporates code from Gester.
Use at your own risk.

> This repository is a community fork of the now-abandoned Maybe Finance project.
> Learn more in their final release doc.
Backstory
The Maybe Finance (archived/abandoned repo) team spent most of 2021–2022 building a full-featured personal finance and wealth management app. It even included an “Ask an Advisor” feature that connected users with a real CFP/CFA — all included with your subscription.
The business end of things didn't work out, and so they stopped developing the app in mid-2023.

TensorFold
TensorFold serves language models from a Zig binary on Apple Silicon and NVIDIA GPUs.
The engine reads checkpoints, tokenizes requests and runs Metal or CUDA kernels directly.
Serving needs no Python or MLX installation.
Building with a coding agent? Have it load the contributor skill before it writes any code.
Contributing with agents
Please use Agent Traffic Control before editing TensorFold so contributors and agents can avoid duplicate work and conflicting changes.
Check the live agent radar before choosing an issue and follow CONTRIBUTING.md and the ATC contributor instructions.
Install or upgrade ATC to 0.9.4 or later, then run from an updated TensorFold clone:
npm install -g github:ashhart/ATC
atc check ISSUE --json
atc claim ISSUE --json
Replace ISSUE with the issue number and claim only after a complete check says the work is free.
TensorFold enables automatic public check-ins: a successful new claim starts an anonymous session on the radar and returns its session number.
Keep that number instead of starting a duplicate session.
For work already yours, start a session with atc start ISSUE --json.
Add --github-name to claim or start only if you want your verified GitHub name shown; --local keeps a new session on your machine.
The board shows the issue, activity state and last check-in; GitHub still associates the verification comment with its author.
Check that publication is public; unavailable means the public update failed even if the local claim or session succeeded.
Pulse only while the agent is working, before its five-minute check-in expires:
atc pulse ISSUE SESSION working --json
atc who path/to/file --json
atc overlap --json
atc land ISSUE SESSION --json
atc release ISSUE --json
Use reviewing or blocked when appropriate, land the session when it stops, and resolve overlaps before opening a pull request.
Before opening a pull request, have the agent run the pull request skill; agents that support skills can install it as tensorfold-pull-request.
Quick start
Start with Qwen3.5-2B, the small 4-bit checkpoint checked on Metal and a GB10. The commands below download its
pinned revision, then serve it as local-model. Model weights have their own licenses.
Reviewing or benchmarking TensorFold? Evaluating TensorFold covers pinning, signature checks,
a container and the tests that need no GPU.
Mac with Apple Silicon
Install with Homebrew, then start the server:
brew install ashhart/tensorfold/tensorfold
tensorfold pull mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit@93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3
tensorfold serve mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit --name local-model --context 8192 --no-thinking
Linux with an NVIDIA GPU
Use the release archive for your CPU: linux-aarch64 on a GB10, linux-x86_64 on an x86_64 host.
It needs glibc 2.28 or newer and NVIDIA driver R580 or newer (CUDA 13.0), providing libcuda.so.1. Keep the archive's directories together.
Its kernels are built with CUDA 13, so TensorFold refuses an older driver at startup; nvidia-smi shows the installed one.
See the CUDA runbook for runtime libraries and supported GPUs.
V=1.2.7
case "$(uname -m)" in
aarch64|arm64) PLATFORM=linux-aarch64 ;;
x86_64) PLATFORM=linux-x86_64 ;;
) echo 'No release archive for this CPU' >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
curl -fLO "https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/releases/download/v$V/tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
curl -fLO "https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/releases/download/v$V/tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256"
sha256sum -c "tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256"
tar -xzf "tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
export PATH="$PWD/tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM/bin:$PATH"
tensorfold() { command tensorfold-native "$@"; }
tensorfold pull mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit@93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3
tensorfold serve mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit --name local-model --context 8192 --no-thinking
Send a request
Leave the server running. In another terminal, on either platform:
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \nH 'Content-Type: application/json' \nd '{"model":"local-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello in one sentence."}],"max_tokens":128,"temperature":0}'
The API also serves completions, Responses and Anthropic Messages. /v1/models lists the served name.
On Windows with an NVIDIA GPU, follow the native Windows build guide.
Use tensorfold --help, tensorfold capabilities --json and tensorfold serve REPO --help to inspect your binary.
You can also serve a complete local checkpoint directory or an existing Hugging Face cache.
tensorfold web [ARGS...] opens TensorFold Web, a small local web app for picking, running and chatting with models.
If it needs installing, an interactive release binary offers to install its matching version with uv after you say yes.
See the web launcher for manual installation and unattended use.
-parallel N caps active requests at N; extra requests wait for a free slot.
Omitting the flag uses --parallel auto, which asks for up to eight streams as memory and the engine allow.
An explicit number is refused if the engine cannot fit that many streams.

With API authentication off, /health reports live.connections as active plus waiting requests and
live.waiting as the queued count. For example, 8 connections with 4 waiting means 4 active requests.
Completing or cancelling an active request frees its slot; cancelling a waiting request removes it from the queue.

Node.js follows semantic versioning.

then are promoted to Current (see below) each April. Alpha releases are signed,

**Current**: Under active development, no semver-major changes allowed. Node.js
releases a new major version once a year, in April. Releases stay Current for
6 months, then convert to LTS (see below) each October. Their ABI may change
between releases. They are intended for library authors and CI pipelines, not
for production use.
**LTS**: Releases under Long Term Support, with a focus on stability
and security. Only changes that have been on Alpha or Current release for two
weeks can be backported to a typical LTS release. Every major version becomes an LTS
release, and receives 30 months of LTS support, for a total of 36 months from
its first Current release to End-of-Life. LTS release lines have alphabetically-ordered
code names, beginning with Node.js 4 Argon.
**Nightly**: Code from the main branch built every 24-hours when there are
changes. Unlike Alpha releases, nightly builds are automated and untested.

Astryx
An open source design system that's fully customizable and built for how we build now: by people and the agents working alongside them.
*Currently in Beta** · Built on React 19+ and StyleX
![npm version](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@astryxdesign/core)
![license MIT](LICENSE)
![PRs welcome](https://github.com/meta/astryx/wiki/Contributing)
![Docs](https://astryx.atmeta.com)
![Storybook](https://astryx.atmeta.com/storybook/)
![Sandbox](https://astryx.atmeta.com/sandbox/)
*Docs** · **Storybook** · **Sandbox** · **Contributing** · **Discord**
Overview
Astryx is an open source design system that grew inside Meta over the last eight years, where it became the most-used and largest design system in the company — powering 13,000+ apps and shaped by the engineers, designers, and product teams who depend on it every day.
It ships 150+ accessible components, brand-level theming, dark mode, ready-to-ship templates, and a CLI as one cohesive system. You import pre-built CSS and use typed React components — no build plugin, no styling library to adopt — and both people and AI assistants build with the same tooling.
*What makes Astryx different:**
**Open internals.** Components are built to be composed at any level, not locked behind a closed top-level API. The building blocks you'd reach for are exported directly, and when you need to go deeper, swizzle ejects a component's full source into your project to own.
**No styling lock-in.** Astryx authors its styles with StyleX, but that's invisible to consumers. Override with className using Tailwind, CSS modules, or plain CSS — whatever your project already uses.
**Customize without wrapping.** A theme is a set of CSS custom property overrides, so a designer can make Astryx unmistakably theirs without forking or wrapping component source.
**Built for people and agents.** The API, docs, and CLI are designed together so a person and an AI assistant build the same way, from the same reference.
Getting Started
Astryx requires **React 19** or later (react and react-dom are peer dependencies of @astryxdesign/core).
Install Astryx, a theme, and its peer dependencies:
npm
npm install @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
npm install -D @astryxdesign/cli
pnpm
pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
pnpm add -D @astryxdesign/cli
yarn
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
yarn add -D @astryxdesign/cli
You can also install the CLI once for your computer, so astryx works in any folder and every coding agent knows Astryx; in a project, it still runs that project's own version:
npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli
Project install, global install, or both? astryx docs global/project-global-or-both compares them (both is recommended), and astryx docs global explains how global mode works.
The simplest setup is a few CSS imports plus a theme provider — no build plugin, no PostCSS or Babel config. See the **@astryxdesign/core README** for the full guide (Next.js, Tailwind, Vite, and CDN).
For reliable CLI access, add a script to your package.json:
"scripts": {
"astryx": "node node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/clients/cli/bin/astryx.mjs"
}
Then use it as npm run astryx -- component --list. This avoids path errors when AI assistants or new developers invoke the CLI directly.
Packages
| Package | Description | README |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| @astryxdesign/core | Components, theme system, and utilities | README |
| @astryxdesign/cli | CLI tooling: component docs, templates, scaffolding, themes, and codemods | README |
| @astryxdesign/build | Build plugins for StyleX source builds | README |
| @astryxdesign/theme-* | Seven ready-made, fully customizable themes (neutral, butter, chocolate, matcha, stone, gothic, y2k) | README |
> @astryxdesign/lab (experimental components) is used internally for Storybook and the sandbox and is not published to npm. @astryxdesign/vega (Vega/Vega-Lite chart wrapper) and @astryxdesign/charts (chart components) are published to npm only under the @canary dist-tag — there is no stable release yet.
Principles
These are the promises Astryx makes to the people building on it.
**Guidance over enforcement.** Components give you capability rather than guardrails that fight you. Design opinions live in docs and examples — if you pass a value, the component renders it.
**Strong, documented conventions.** Every component follows the same naming, prop, and composition rules, and every one is thoroughly documented — so once you've learned a few, the rest feel familiar, and both people and AI can predict how an unfamiliar component behaves.
**One system for humans and AI.** The API, conventions, docs, and CLI are designed together so people and AI assistants build the same way. Every change that made Astryx easier for AI made it easier for people too.
**Earned by measurement.** We test conventions rather than assert them, hold the results loosely, and revisit them when a new situation proves them wrong.
Architecture
Foundations
The building blocks for visually cohesive and accessible interfaces: typography, color, layout, and accessibility.
Components
A library of 150+ reusable UI building blocks with full TypeScript support.
Patterns
Battle-tested design solutions for common interactions and workflows: table pages, detail page layouts, form wizards, navigation patterns, data entry flows.
Project Structure
| Directory | Purpose |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| apps/ | Example apps, the docsite, and Storybook |
| packages/ | Published packages: core, cli, build, themes |
| internal/ | Internal tooling: test utilities, eslint plugin, vibe tests |
Contributing
We welcome contributions! See **CONTRIBUTING.md** for the full guide.
Questions, or want a hand with a PR? Come find us in
*Discord**.
Our conventions and review rubrics live in the
Contributing wiki —
including API Conventions,
Design Conventions,
the Component Lifecycle,
the Contributing Templates,
and the Blog Review Rubric. Read the relevant rubric before opening a PR.
Quick start for contributors: this repo uses **Node 22+ on an active LTS line**
and **pnpm 11**. Install pnpm directly, or enable
Corepack once so the pinned pnpm version

Getting started
On your laptop
The easiest way to get started is with the fully self-contained app that runs on your laptop, combining the OpenBot frontend and Docker-based backend in one application.
Mac / Apple silicon · Mac / Intel · Windows
Run from source
For your team
*OpenBot for Business** brings your agents into one workspace with company sign-in, tool permissions, approvals, and audit. Deploy on your infrastructure or work with our engineers on hosting and customization.
*Get early access to OpenBot for Business →** · **Talk to an engineer** · **Kubernetes setup**
Web, mobile, and chat
Web · iOS · Android · Slack · Teams
Your workspace. Your stack.
**Choose your models.** Use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, or open models through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, hosted by a provider or on your own infrastructure. Keep your provider relationships and change models as your needs change.
**Bring your agents.** Run built-in Bots in the OpenBot server, or connect your existing agents through AG-UI from any agent execution platform. Agents built with different stacks can work in the same workspace.
**Make it yours.** Use the MIT-licensed template as-is, white-label it, or customize it deeply. AG-UI connects agents, MCP connects tools, and the frontends and backend can evolve independently.
**Govern work across your team.** Company sign-in, roles, tool permissions, approvals, and audit apply across the workspace. Your agents use OpenBot's tools and computers under the same policies.
**Get help deploying it.** CopilotKit's engineers can work with your team to deploy OpenBot, connect your systems, and automate parts of specific jobs.
Connect your agent · Configure models and tools · Explore OpenBot for Business
Built on CopilotKit and AG-UI
OpenBot is built on CopilotKit, which is used in production by a majority of Fortune 500 companies.
*Your agent stack.** AG-UI has first-class integrations across the major agent frameworks and harnesses, including Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework and Agent Harness, Google ADK, AWS Strands, Oracle Agent Spec, LangChain, Mastra, Pydantic AI, Agno, and CrewAI. Many ship first-party support; Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supports AG-UI directly.
*Your execution platform.** Keep your agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Managed Agents, Google's Agent Platform, LangChain's Managed Deep Agents, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service, or your own infrastructure. Connect them to OpenBot through an AG-UI endpoint, using an adapter where needed. Your choice of agent platform stays independent of your workspace.
Architecture
OpenBot has three parts. On your laptop, setup runs the backend and Intelligence for you. For a team, the Helm chart deploys both on Kubernetes in your own infrastructure.
| Part | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **OpenBot frontends** | Mac, Windows, web, iOS, Android, Slack, and Teams connect people to the same workspace. Conversations, interactive results, computer view, and approvals adapt to each surface. Choose a frontend. |
| **OpenBot backend** | Runs the workspace API and built-in Bots, connects external agents and tools, manages Bot computers, and enforces identity, permissions, action policies, and audit. Deploys on Kubernetes with PostgreSQL and persistent storage. |
| **CopilotKit Intelligence** | Durable conversations, memory, Automatic Learning, and enterprise governance services. Separately licensed; runs on Kubernetes alongside OpenBot. |
OpenBot enforces sign-in, tool permissions, action policies, and audit at its API, alongside Intelligence's platform services. Built-in Bots run in the OpenBot server; your own agents can run alongside OpenBot or on any agent execution platform. Both use AG-UI and can share the same workspace.
Computer execution is pluggable: use the default Kubernetes setup or connect a compatible external computer provider.
Architecture details · Services and ports · Kubernetes deployment
Open source, local operation, and licensing
*The OpenBot application template is open source under the MIT license.** You can fork, modify, and white-label it. It uses **CopilotKit Intelligence**, which is separately licensed and can run entirely on your own machine or infrastructure.
| Where you run it | CopilotKit Intelligence license |
| --- | --- |
| **Your laptop, for personal use and experimentation** | Requires a free local Intelligence license. Desktop setup handles this for you. |
| **Kubernetes evaluation** | Requires a free Intelligence trial license. Request a trial. |
| **Kubernetes / production** | Requires a production Intelligence license beyond evaluation. OpenBot for Business includes Intelligence for use with OpenBot. Plans and pricing. |
*Fully local is an option.** Run OpenBot, Intelligence, and a compatible model locally. A cloud model or connected online app still sends requests to that service. Initial downloads, account sign-in, and local license renewal need internet access.
--
Deploy on Kubernetes
Deploy OpenBot and CopilotKit Intelligence together on **AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE, or your own Kubernetes cluster**. The chart installs Intelligence by default; no separate hosted project is required.
For a first evaluation, you need a cluster with **amd64 nodes**, a **default StorageClass**, kubectl, Helm, a **trial or production license**, and a model key. The commands below use an OpenAI key. For Anthropic, a model router, cluster sizing, or an existing Intelligence deployment, use the full Helm guide.
> **Setting up with an AI assistant?** Give it this README and the Helm guide. The guide covers cloud-specific values, storage, secrets, sign-in, networking, upgrades, and troubleshooting. Use the evaluation below only through a local port-forward; configure sign-in and TLS before sharing a deployment.

git clone https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot.git
cd OpenBot

secrets:
licenseToken: ""
modelApiKey: ""

helm dependency build charts/openbot
helm install openbot charts/openbot \n-namespace openbot --create-namespace \n-values charts/openbot/ci/vanilla-values.yaml \n-values openbot-secrets.yaml \n-timeout 15m
4. **Open your evaluation.**
kubectl -n openbot get pods,jobs
kubectl -n openbot port-forward svc/openbot-server 3001:3001
Open . This configuration is single-user: anyone who can reach it is an administrator. Keep the port-forward local.

Description
The main goal of llama.cpp is to enable LLM (and VLM) inference with minimal setup and state-of-the-art performance on
a wide range of hardware - locally and in the cloud.
Plain C/C++ implementation without any dependencies
Apple silicon is a first-class citizen - optimized via ARM NEON, Accelerate and Metal frameworks
AVX, AVX2, AVX512 and AMX support for x86 architectures
RVV, ZVFH, ZFH, ZICBOP and ZIHINTPAUSE support for RISC-V architectures
1.5-bit, 2-bit, 3-bit, 4-bit, 5-bit, 6-bit, and 8-bit integer quantization for faster inference and reduced memory use
Custom CUDA kernels for running LLMs on NVIDIA GPUs (support for AMD GPUs via HIP and Moore Threads GPUs via MUSA)
Vulkan and SYCL backend support
CPU+GPU hybrid inference to partially accelerate models larger than the total VRAM capacity
The llama.cpp project is build on top of the ggml library.
